comparison: Both evaluations agree that TIM23 core component reduction (C2, C31, C32, C33, C39) is well-supported by immunoblotting evidence. Peer reviewers explicitly state the authors 'provide compelling evidence' and experiments are 'of high quality.' OpenEval notes convergence across two model systems. Peer review also includes C34-C36, C40 in this group, which OpenEval evaluates separately in R2.

Both agree that PAM subunit levels remain unchanged (C34-C36, C40). OpenEval notes this is surprising given expected TIM23 dependence but well-documented. Peer reviewers accept these findings without critique as part of their overall positive assessment of the immunoblotting data.

Both address the finding that most proteins remain unaffected (C3, C37, C42, C43, C55, C112). OpenEval finds the proteomics data well-supported despite being counterintuitive. Peer reviewers accept the data but Reviewer 2 explicitly questions the mechanism, noting 'it remains somewhat unclear why this is,' suggesting possible compensation or non-rate-limiting import. This represents a key difference in interpretation confidence.

Both evaluations express uncertainty about the mechanistic inference (C4, C112) that TIM23 is not rate-limiting for most proteins. OpenEval notes alternative explanations are not excluded. Peer reviewers similarly question the mechanism, with Reviewer 2 suggesting compensation or non-rate-limiting import as possibilities. Strong agreement on uncertainty.

Both strongly support the selective downregulation of OXPHOS and MRP subunits (C7, C8, C49-C51, C56, C113). OpenEval emphasizes mass spectrometry data and replication across models. Peer Reviewer 1 calls this 'surprising and highly interesting' and provides 'compelling evidence.' Strong concordance on this key finding.

Both support the mechanistic inference about MRP reduction affecting mitochondrial translation (C52, C53). OpenEval finds the logic reasonable given normal OXA insertase levels. Peer reviewers accept this interpretation as part of the direct mechanism, with Reviewer 1 noting findings 'shed new light on mitochondrial biogenesis.'

Both support the control experiment ruling out mtDNA loss (C59-C61). OpenEval notes this appropriately excludes an alternative explanation. Peer reviewers accept this as part of evidence that effects are direct rather than indirect, supporting the overall mechanistic interpretation.

Both strongly support respiratory impairment findings (C9, C62-C68). OpenEval emphasizes Seahorse data replication across both model systems. Peer reviewers accept these functional consequences as 'convincing' evidence with 'high quality' experiments. Strong agreement on functional validation.

Both support ATP reduction findings (C10, C84). OpenEval notes direct measurement in neurons with inference for fibroblasts. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the overall convincing functional evidence without specific concerns about the ATP measurements.

Perfect agreement on glycolytic impairment (C69-C75). Both evaluations support the Seahorse glycolysis stress test data showing reduced capacity and reserves. OpenEval notes cells cannot compensate for OXPHOS defects. Peer reviewers accept as part of high-quality metabolic characterization. Complete concordance.

Both support mitochondrial trafficking defects (C11, C77-C80). OpenEval validates the live cell imaging methodology and quantitative parameters. Peer reviewers implicitly accept by acknowledging the study's use of both model systems to investigate impacts. Both also accept the ATP-related mechanistic interpretation (C82, C83, C102).

Both support the inference linking ATP deficiency to trafficking defects (C82, C83, C102). OpenEval notes the logic is sound given intact machinery but reduced ATP, though causation not directly demonstrated. Peer reviewers accept this mechanistic interpretation as consistent with overall conclusions.

Both strongly support increased neuronal firing and electrophysiological changes (C13, C86-C92). OpenEval validates the comprehensive patch clamp characterization. Peer Reviewer 1 calls this 'surprising and highly interesting' with 'compelling evidence.' Strong concordance on this key neuronal phenotype.

Both support potassium channel reduction findings (C14, C94, C95). OpenEval emphasizes convergence of mass spectrometry and immunoblot methods. Peer reviewers highlight this as a key finding with 'compelling evidence,' accepting the multi-method validation approach.

Both support the pharmacological validation with α-DTX (C96-C98). OpenEval finds the experiment appropriately tests KCNA2's functional contribution. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the compelling evidence for potassium channel involvement in the firing phenotype.

Strong agreement on uncertainty about linking mouse model findings to human epilepsy (C15, C104, C111, C116). OpenEval notes the direct link is not experimentally validated and patient neurons were not tested. Peer reviewers similarly note 'mechanisms...remain unexplained,' accepting correlation but questioning causal explanation. Complete concordance on uncertainty.

Both express uncertainty about connections between cellular phenotypes and patient clinical symptoms (C12, C81, C103, C115). OpenEval notes causal links are not directly tested and remain hypothetical. Peer reviewers find cellular effects convincing but note clinical connections are inferential, with Reviewer 2 suggesting future investigation needed. Agreement on speculative nature.

Both express uncertainty about the mechanistic speculation regarding TIM23 complex assembly (C99-C101). OpenEval notes the observation is intriguing but mechanism not investigated, with alternative explanations unexplored. Peer reviewers similarly note mechanisms 'remain unexplained' and 'somewhat unclear.' Strong agreement on need for further mechanistic investigation.

Disagreement on the inference about complex protein import specificity (C114). OpenEval expresses uncertainty, noting the mechanism is not directly tested and requires validation through import/assembly studies. Peer reviewers support this interpretation as part of the accepted mechanistic framework, with Reviewer 1 noting findings 'shed new light on mitochondrial biogenesis.' Key difference in confidence.

Both support the observation of upregulated matrix proteins (C44-C47). OpenEval notes the finding is unexpected but well-documented, though biological significance unclear. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the selective protein changes, with Reviewer 1 highlighting the selective nature of substrate effects as a key observation.

OpenEval evaluates the comparison between fibroblasts and neurons showing different proteome impacts (C57, C58), attributing differences to temporal exposure. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing this specific cross-system comparison.

OpenEval evaluates background knowledge claims (C1, C5, C16-C30, C76, C85, C93, C96, C105-C110) as appropriately cited established knowledge. Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate these contextual/background claims.

OpenEval expresses uncertainty about therapeutic implications claim (C117), noting it is aspirational rather than evidence-based with no interventions tested. Peer reviewers do not separately address this speculative therapeutic statement.
